::: {.chapter-goal}
#### In this chapter
You will follow an outbreak through a forest, one summer at a time: the bark beetle epidemic that killed most of the spruce in the Harz mountains of Germany after the 2018 drought. For every conifer pixel you will find the year its canopy dried out, map how the damage spread, and test whether satellites saw the trees dying before they were recorded as lost. They did not, at least not with annual data, and that negative result is worth as much as the map.
:::

## Why a German forest in an Indonesian book

Pests and diseases kill trees in Indonesia too: root rot in plantations, fungal wilt in acacia, pests that defoliate teak. But few of these outbreaks have open, well-documented data. The Harz outbreak is one of the best-documented forest disturbances of the satellite era: a hot drought in 2018, weakened spruce, and a bark beetle population that exploded over the following years. Across Germany, canopy cover loss from January 2018 to April 2021 reached about 501,000 ha, with the largest losses in the centre of the country [@thonfeld2022canopy]. The method you learn here carries over to any outbreak where the canopy dries before it dies.

## How an outbreak looks from above

Bark beetles bore under the bark and cut the tree's water transport. The needles stay green for a while (*green attack*), then turn red, then grey, and fall. From space the clearest signal is **canopy water**: the normalised difference moisture index,

$$\text{NDMI} = \frac{\text{NIR} - \text{SWIR}}{\text{NIR} + \text{SWIR}},$$

falls as the needles dry and the canopy thins (P1: water absorbs shortwave infrared).

The method:

1. **Conifer forest**: needle-leaved evergreen forest in the Copernicus 2019 land cover, with at least 50 % tree cover in 2000 (Hansen).
2. **One number per summer**: the median NDMI of June to August, every year from 2017 to 2024 (Sentinel-2, Cloud Score+ masked). Summer avoids snow and the seasonal cycle.
3. **Onset**: the first summer in which a pixel's NDMI falls more than 0.15 below its own 2017 value, *and stays down the following summer*, so a single dry summer that recovers is not counted.
4. **Check**: the year Hansen first records the pixel as tree cover loss.

Before trusting any year-to-year comparison, count the images: summer 2017 has 36 Sentinel-2 scenes over the area and full coverage, later summers about 75. The baseline is sound (compare the 2018 trap in Chapter [-@sec-enforcement]).

{{< include _snippets/ch58_forest_dieback.qmd >}}

## Reading the results

**The outbreak in numbers.** Of about 48,000 ha of conifer forest in the study area, about **34,100 ha (71 %) had dried out and stayed dry by 2024**. The wave was small in 2018 (about 1,600 ha), grew in 2019 (4,000 ha), peaked in **2020 (about 11,900 ha)**, and was still large in 2021 and 2022 (8,800 and 6,000 ha). By 2023 and 2024 almost no new area was affected, mostly because little healthy spruce was left.

**Every cohort tells the same story in its own year.** Group the pixels by onset year and plot their mean NDMI. Each group stays near its 2017 level, then collapses in its onset year, from about 0.4 to about 0.1, and stays low. In 2024 the oldest cohorts rise a little again: young trees and ground vegetation grow on the dead or cleared stands. Even the never-stressed conifers dip slightly in the dry summers of 2018, 2020 and 2022, which is why the threshold is 0.15 and why the drop has to last.

**The map shows spread, not just damage.** Read the onset map as a sequence. The early patches (2018–2019, dark blue) are scattered through the centre and east of the area; the later years (2021–2022, lighter greens) are more common in the south and west, filling the gaps between older patches; and most of the conifer that stayed healthy lies in the west. Whether the early patches share something (lower elevation, south-facing slopes, stand edges) is a question for a terrain layer and a test, not for the eye (exercise 4). That pattern of spread is what a forest manager needs to plan where to look next.

**No early warning, and why.** The hope was that the canopy would dry *before* the trees were recorded as lost, giving managers a year to act. It did not happen here. For 68 % of the stressed pixels, Hansen records the loss in the same year as our onset or earlier; 22 % one year later; only a few percent later still. Two reasons. First, Hansen's "tree cover loss" includes standing dead trees, not only cutting, so it sees the same dieback we do. Second, one number per summer is too coarse: the green-attack stage lasts weeks, and by the next summer the canopy is already red or gone. Real early warning needs sub-annual time series, red-edge bands that respond to chlorophyll, and field checks of the first suspicious patches.

## From the Harz to Indonesian plantations

The same three steps apply to a disease outbreak in an acacia or oil-palm plantation, with three changes:

- **No snow, no summer**: in the tropics, use a moving baseline (the same months of earlier years) or a harmonic model of the season (Chapter [-@sec-timeseries]), not one summer.
- **Clouds**: monthly optical composites will have gaps; Sentinel-1 radar can fill some of them, though it responds to structure, not water in the leaves.
- **Harvest is not disease**: plantations are cut on purpose. A drop followed by bare soil and replanting is a harvest; a slow decline in a stand that should be growing is the suspicious signal (Chapter [-@sec-oil-palm-age]).

## Exercises {.unnumbered}

1. Change the threshold from 0.15 to 0.10 and 0.20. How does the area of the outbreak change, and which threshold produces patches that make sense on the map?
2. Replace the summer median with monthly medians for 2019–2020 and look for a pixel whose NDMI falls months before the Hansen loss year.
3. Run the same script for a beech (broadleaf) forest nearby. Did the 2018 drought stress it too, and did it recover?
4. Add elevation and aspect (Chapter [-@sec-terrain]) and compare the early-onset pixels (2018–2019) with the late ones (2021–2022). Is the difference real or within the noise?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answers

**1.** Not computed in the chapter. At 0.10 more pixels qualify, including stands that only browned or thinned, so the outbreak area grows and patches become noisier, with isolated pixels scattered through healthy forest. At 0.20 only the most severe drying counts, the area shrinks and late or partial damage is missed. The threshold that makes sense is the one whose patches are compact and spread outward from earlier patches year by year, as a beetle outbreak does; usually that is near 0.15.

**2.** Not computed in the chapter. Compute monthly NDMI medians from April 2019 to October 2020 for pixels whose Hansen loss year is 2020 or 2021. Look for a drop below the pixel's own 2017 level in the summer or autumn before the loss year: red-attack crowns dry out before salvage felling removes them, so the satellite often sees the damage months before Hansen records loss, which is when the stand was cut, not when it died.

**3.** Not computed in the chapter. Select broadleaf forest in the Copernicus land cover and run the same summer-NDMI script. Expect beech to show a drop in 2018 and 2019 (drought stress, early leaf fall) followed largely by recovery from 2020, without the permanent collapse of spruce: broadleaf trees are hit by the drought but not by the spruce bark beetle. The one-summer rule ("stays down the following summer") is what separates stress from death.

**4.** Not computed in the chapter. Sample elevation and aspect for early-onset (2018-2019) and late-onset (2021-2022) pixels and compare their distributions with a test that accounts for spatial clustering (block resampling, since neighbouring pixels are not independent). Early outbreaks often start on warmer, lower, south-facing slopes where drought stress is greatest; if the difference survives the block test it is real, if not it is within the noise of neighbouring pixels.
:::
